questions.question: Q: What is the difference between HBV and LBV proteins?
questions.correctAnswer: HBV (high biological value) proteins contain all 9 essential amino acids and come mainly from animal sources (meat, fish, eggs, dairy) and soya. LBV (low biological value) proteins lack one or more essential amino acids and come from plant sources (cereals, pulses, nuts). LBV proteins can be combined (complementary proteins) to provide all essential amino acids.

questions.question: Q: Explain why saturated and unsaturated fats have different health effects.
questions.correctAnswer: Saturated fats (animal sources, solid at room temperature) raise LDL ('bad') cholesterol, increasing heart disease risk. Unsaturated fats (plant and fish sources, liquid at room temperature) can help lower LDL cholesterol and raise HDL ('good') cholesterol, reducing heart disease risk. Public health advice recommends replacing saturated with unsaturated fats.

questions.question: Q: Evaluate the importance of dietary fibre in the diet.
questions.correctAnswer: Fibre is essential for digestive health — it adds bulk to stools, prevents constipation, and feeds beneficial gut bacteria. It reduces risk of bowel cancer, heart disease, and type 2 diabetes. However, excessive fibre can interfere with mineral absorption. The UK average intake (14g/day) is well below the recommended 30g/day, making increased fibre consumption a public health priority.

questions.correctAnswer: Macronutrients — carbohydrates, proteins, and fats — each play essential roles in maintaining health, and balance between them is crucial. Carbohydrates provide the body's primary energy source. Glucose from carbohydrate digestion fuels the brain and muscles. Complex carbohydrates (wholegrains, pulses) also provide dietary fibre, essential for digestive health and reducing risk of bowel cancer and type 2 diabetes. Current UK guidelines recommend carbohydrates provide about 50% of dietary energy. Proteins are vital for growth, repair, and maintenance of body tissues. HBV proteins from animal sources provide all essential amino acids, while LBV plant proteins can be combined to achieve the same effect. Protein deficiency causes kwashiorkor and marasmus, though these are rare in developed countries. Fats provide concentrated energy and carry fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K). However, the type of fat matters significantly: unsaturated fats (olive oil, oily fish) reduce cardiovascular risk, while excess saturated fats (butter, fatty meat) raise LDL cholesterol and increase heart disease risk. The balance between macronutrients is key. The Eatwell Guide recommends roughly 50% energy from carbohydrates, 35% from fats (mostly unsaturated), and 15% from protein. Most UK diets contain too much saturated fat and sugar, and insufficient fibre, contributing to obesity and chronic diseases.
